entry: Capital and largest city of [[Jordan]] (pop., 2026: five million), and the country's economic, political and cultural center. Settlement dates to at least the 8th millennium BC at 'Ain Ghazal, a [[Neolithic]] site with the world's oldest human statues. As Rabbath Ammon, capital of the Ammonite Kingdom, the city was known in the Hellenistic, Nabataean and Roman periods as Philadelphia; the [[Rashidun Caliphate]] renamed it Amman in the 7th century. It was resettled by [[Circassians]] in 1878 and became a commercial center after the Hejaz Railway. Designated capital of Transjordan in 1921, it grew rapidly after waves of refugees from Palestine, Iraq and Syria. Built on seven hills, it now spans 19 hills and 22 areas, administered by the Greater Amman Municipality.

Inorganic chemical compound of nitrogen and hydrogen, with the formula NH₃. A colorless gas with a distinctive pungent smell, it is widely used in [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], refrigerants, explosives and cleaning agents, and as a precursor for numerous chemicals. About 70% of industrially produced ammonia is used to make fertilizers such as [[Urea|urea]] and diammonium phosphate. Ammonia is produced biologically by nitrogen fixation, but most is made by the [[Haber process]], which provided cheap fertilizers and helped revolutionize agriculture. Conventional production accounts for about 500 million tons a year of CO₂ emissions. Global industrial production was 235 million metric tons in 2021. Ammonia is toxic, and most animals excrete it as dissolved urea. It boils at −33.34 °C at one atmosphere. Household ammonia is a solution of ammonia in water.

Inorganic salt of ammonium and chloride, NH₄Cl. It is a white crystalline salt, highly soluble in water, whose solutions are mildly acidic. The naturally occurring mineral form, salammoniac, forms on burning coal dumps and around some volcanic vents. Commercially it is made by reacting [[Ammonia|ammonia]] with hydrochloric acid or hydrogen chloride. Its dominant use is as a nitrogen [[Fertilizer|fertilizer]], accounting for 90% of world production, mainly on rice and wheat in Asia. It is also used as a food additive.

White crystalline salt of ammonium and nitrate ions, NH₄NO₃, highly soluble in water and hygroscopic as a solid. It is used predominantly in agriculture as a high-nitrogen [[Fertilizer|fertilizer]], and as a component of [[Explosive|explosive mixtures]] used in mining, quarrying and civil construction. It is the major constituent of ANFO, an industrial explosive which accounts for 80% of explosives used in North America; similar formulations have been used in [[Improvised explosive device|improvised explosive devices]]. Many countries are phasing out its use in consumer applications because of its potential for misuse. Accidental explosions have killed thousands of people since the early 20th century. Global production was estimated at 21.6 million tonnes in 2017 and was down to 16.7 million tonnes by 2021. It is made by reacting [[Ammonia|ammonia]] with [[Nitric acid|nitric acid]]. Mining of natural deposits in Chile's Atacama Desert ended once the [[Haber process|Haber–Bosch process]] made synthetic nitrates possible.

Inorganic salt, (NH₄)₂SO₄, with a number of commercial uses. It contains 21% nitrogen and 24% sulfur. Its most common use is as a [[Fertilizer|soil fertilizer]], particularly for alkaline soils, where the released ammonium ion forms a small amount of acid that lowers soil pH. Its low nitrogen content relative to [[Ammonium nitrate|ammonium nitrate]] or [[Urea|urea]] raises transport costs. It is also an agricultural spray adjuvant for several herbicides. In the laboratory, ammonium sulfate precipitation is a common method of protein purification, since proteins become less soluble as ionic strength rises. It is generally recognized as safe (GRAS) by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and is designated E517 in the European Union. It is made by treating [[Ammonia|ammonia]] with [[Sulfuric acid|sulfuric acid]]; approximately 6,000 million tons were produced in 1981.

Material fired, scattered, dropped or detonated from a weapon or weapon system, also known as ammo. Its expendable forms include [[Bomb|bombs]], [[Missile|missiles]], [[Grenade|grenades]] and [[Land mine|land mines]], as well as the parts of other weapons that create the effect on a target, such as bullets and warheads. A firearm cartridge contains all components required to deliver the weapon's effect in one package. Black powder was the most common propellant until the 20th century and has since been replaced in nearly all cases by modern compounds. Internationally recognized standards, such as 5.56×45mm NATO, allow some types to be used across different weapons. A dud is ammunition that fails to function as intended. Duds are classified as unexploded ordnance and remain dangerous; large quantities of [[World War I]] ammunition are still found in France and Belgium.

Deficit in [[Memory|memory]] caused by [[Brain injury|brain damage]] or disease, or temporarily by sedative and hypnotic drugs. Memory may be wholly or partly lost, depending on the extent of damage. Retrograde amnesia is the inability to remember information acquired before a particular date, usually the date of an accident or operation, and may extend back decades. Anterograde amnesia is the inability to transfer new information from short-term to long-term storage. The two types may occur together. Other forms include transient global amnesia, dissociative amnesia linked to emotional stress, childhood amnesia, and post-traumatic amnesia following a head injury. Amnesia is typically associated with damage to the medial temporal lobe and the [[Hippocampus|hippocampus]]. Many people with amnesia can still learn new procedural knowledge.

Unicellular organism or cell type that changes shape, mainly by extending and retracting pseudopods. Amoebae do not form a single taxonomic group; they occur in every major lineage of eukaryotic organisms, and amoeboid cells also occur in fungi, algae and animals. Amoebae have no cell walls and feed by phagocytosis, engulfing food particles with pseudopods. Free-living forms may be naked or testate, enclosed in a shell. Most freshwater species have a contractile [[Vacuole|vacuole]] that expels excess water. The best-known species, *Amoeba proteus* and *Chaos carolinense*, are widely studied in laboratories. *Naegleria fowleri* is the so-called 'brain-eating amoeba', and *Entamoeba histolytica* is an intestinal parasite that causes amoebic dysentery. The multicellular 'social amoeba' *Dictyostelium discoideum* is a [[Slime mold|slime mold]].

Major taxonomic group of about 2,400 described species of amoeboid [[Protist|protists]]. Its members often have blunt, fingerlike, lobose pseudopods and tubular mitochondrial cristae. Traditionally ranked as a phylum within the kingdom Protista or Protozoa, it is retained by the International Society of Protistologists as an unranked 'supergroup' within [[Eukaryote|Eukaryota]]. Molecular analysis supports it as a monophyletic [[Clade|clade]] and the sister group to Opisthokonta, which includes fungi and animals; the two are sometimes grouped as Amorphea. The group includes Chaos, Entamoeba, Pelomyxa and the genus [[Amoeba]], as well as several clades of slime molds. Species may be shelled or naked, and cells may possess flagella. Most are unicellular, though some slime molds form a macroscopic plasmodium. Some are parasites, and some cause disease in humans.

Ancient Northwest Semitic-speaking [[Bronze Age]] people from western [[Mesopotamia]]. First mentioned in Sumerian records c. 2500 BC, they ruled most of the [[Levant]] and Mesopotamia, and parts of Egypt, from the 21st century BC to the start of the 16th century BC. Amorite city-states included Isin, Kurda, Larsa, Mari and [[Ebla]], and the Amorites founded [[Babylon]] and the Old Babylonian Empire. They also founded the Fourteenth Dynasty of Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period, and were likely part of the later Hyksos. In Akkadian and Sumerian texts, Amurru refers to the Amorites, their principal deity and their kingdom. Some Akkadian literature speaks disparagingly of them as nomads. The Hebrew Bible describes them as inhabitants of [[Canaan]] before and after the conquest under Joshua. Shu-Sin of the Third Dynasty of Ur built a 270 km wall between the Tigris and Euphrates to hold them off.

Solid that lacks the long-range order characteristic of a [[Crystal|crystal]]. Also called a non-crystalline solid, it includes [[Glass|glasses]], metallic glasses, and certain [[Plastic|plastics]] and [[Polymer|polymers]]. The terms 'glass' and 'glassy solid' are sometimes used as synonyms, but refer specifically to amorphous materials that undergo a glass transition. Amorphous materials show short-range order over typically 1–2 atomic spacings, but no repeating unit cell, so statistical measures such as the radial distribution function describe their structure. The freezing of a liquid into an amorphous solid is one of the important unsolved problems of physics. Below about 1–10 K, amorphous solids share anomalous properties, including nearly linear specific heat and nearly quadratic thermal conductivity, that current theories explain only partly.

Base quantity of the [[International System of Units|International System of Units (SI)]], defined as the ratio of the number of elementary entities in a sample to the [[Avogadro constant]]. Its SI unit is the [[Mole (unit)|mole]] (mol). Since 2019 the Avogadro constant has been defined as exactly 6.02214076×10²³ mol⁻¹, which makes the mole convenient for laboratory-scale chemistry. The entities are usually [[Molecule|molecules]], atoms, ions or ion pairs. The amount of a substance can be calculated from measured mass or volume, given its molar mass or the molar volume of an ideal gas. Because of how the mole and the [[Dalton (unit)|dalton]] are defined, a mole of water has a mass of about 18.0153 grams, close to the mass of one water molecule in daltons. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry deprecates the term 'number of moles'.

Aminopenicillin [[Antibiotic|antibiotic]] of the penicillin family. It is used to treat and prevent bacterial infections such as middle ear infection, strep throat, pneumonia, skin infections and urinary tract infections. Common adverse effects include nausea and rash. It should not be used by people allergic to [[Penicillin|penicillin]]. Discovered in 1958 and in medical use from 1972, it is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines and is one of the most commonly prescribed antibiotics in children.

[[International System of Units|SI]] base unit of electric current, equal to one [[Coulomb|coulomb]] of charge passing a point per second. It is named after French mathematician and physicist [[André-Marie Ampère]], who with [[Hans Christian Ørsted]] is considered the father of [[Electromagnetism|electromagnetism]]. Since the 2019 revision of the SI, the ampere is defined by fixing the elementary charge at exactly 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ coulombs, so one ampere corresponds to about 6.241509074×10¹⁸ elementary charges per second. Previously it was defined by the force between two parallel wires one meter apart in a vacuum, equal to 2×10⁻⁷ newtons per meter of length. An international convention signed at the 1881 International Exposition of Electricity established the ampere as a standard unit.

Central nervous system (CNS) [[Stimulant|stimulant]] used to treat [[Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder|attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)]] and [[Narcolepsy|narcolepsy]]. In the form of lisdexamfetamine it is also used to treat binge eating disorder, and it has historically been used for nasal congestion and depression. Amphetamine was discovered as a chemical in 1887 and as a drug in the late 1920s; the first pharmaceutical form was Benzedrine. It exists as two enantiomers, levoamphetamine and dextroamphetamine. It increases monoamine and excitatory neurotransmission, with its most pronounced effects on the [[Dopamine|dopamine]] and norepinephrine systems. At therapeutic doses it causes euphoria, increased wakefulness and improved cognitive control. [[Addiction|Addiction]] is a serious risk with heavy recreational use, but is unlikely from long-term medical use at therapeutic doses.

Electronic device or circuit that increases the magnitude of a signal, such as a voltage or current. Its [[Gain (electronics)|gain]], the ratio of output to input, measures the amplification; a circuit is an amplifier if its power gain is greater than one. Audio amplifiers handle signals below 20 kHz, radio-frequency amplifiers 20 kHz to 300 GHz, and some servo and instrumentation amplifiers work down to [[Direct current|direct current]]. A preamplifier precedes other signal-processing stages, while a power amplifier provides the final output. The triode [[Vacuum tube|vacuum tube]], invented in 1906 by [[Lee de Forest]], led to the first amplifiers around 1912. Vacuum tubes were used in almost all amplifiers until the 1960s–1970s, when [[Transistor|transistors]] replaced them.

Measure of change in a periodic variable over one period, or of the magnitude of a non-periodic signal relative to a reference value. Peak-to-peak amplitude is the change between peak and trough, written Vpp when applied to voltages, and is often read on an [[Oscilloscope|oscilloscope]]. Semi-amplitude is half of that. Most scientific literature uses 'amplitude' or 'peak amplitude' to mean semi-amplitude. In astronomy, semi-amplitude is the most widely used measure of orbital wobble, and small radial velocity semi-amplitudes help in the search for [[Exoplanet|exoplanets]]. Root mean square (RMS) amplitude is used especially in [[Electrical engineering|electrical engineering]], because the average power transmitted by a wave is proportional to the square of the RMS amplitude. For [[Alternating current|alternating current]] power, the universal practice is to specify RMS values of a sinusoidal waveform.

Removal of a limb or other body part by trauma, medical illness or surgery. Surgical amputation controls pain or disease in the affected limb, such as malignancy or [[Gangrene|gangrene]], and is sometimes performed preventively. Congenital amputation occurs when fetal limbs are cut off by constrictive bands. In some countries, judicial amputation is used to punish crimes, and amputation has been used as a tactic in war and terrorism. The oldest evidence comes from a skeleton in Liang Tebo cave, East Kalimantan, in Indonesian [[Borneo]], dating back at least 31,000 years, where the amputation was done when the person was a young child. A [[Prosthesis|prosthesis]] or bioelectric replantation may restore sensation of the amputated limb.

Arab military commander and companion of [[Muhammad]], who led the Muslim conquest of [[Egypt]] and served as its governor. Son of a wealthy Qurayshite, he embraced Islam c. 629. Caliph [[Abu Bakr]] appointed him to command the conquest of Syria, and he took most of [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]], where he became governor. He helped lead Arab forces to victories over the Byzantines at Ajnadayn and the Yarmuk in 634 and 636. He launched the conquest of Egypt on his own initiative in late 639, and [[Alexandria]] surrendered in 641 or 642. He founded Fustat as the provincial capital, with the mosque later named after him at its center. He governed Egypt in 640–646 and 658–664. Caliph [[Uthman]] dismissed him in 646 after accusations of incompetence. In the First Fitna he joined [[Mu'awiya I|Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan]] against [[Ali|Caliph Ali]], and after Ali's loyalists were defeated he again took control of Egypt.

City in the [[India|Indian]] state of Punjab, second-largest after Ludhiana (pop., 2011: 1,132,383). Located in the Majha region, it is a major cultural, transportation and economic center, and the economic capital of Punjab. It is the administrative headquarters of Amritsar district and lies 28 km from the India–Pakistan border. It is home to the [[Golden Temple|Golden Temple]], the holiest site and most-visited gurdwara in [[Sikhism]]. The city takes its name from the Amṛta Sarovar, the pool surrounding the temple. Guru Ram Das, the fourth Sikh guru, is credited with founding it in 1574, when it was sometimes known as Ramdaspur. In 1919 British forces fired on unarmed protesters in the [[Jallianwala Bagh massacre|Jallianwala Bagh massacre]], killing at least 379 people according to official British reports. The city is known for wooden chessboards and chess pieces.

Capital and largest city of the [[Netherlands]] (pop., 2026: 941,873), in the province of North Holland. Founded at the mouth of the Amstel River, which was dammed to control flooding, it was a small fishing village in the 12th century before becoming a major port during the [[Dutch Golden Age]] of the 17th century. Its canals are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the canal houses with gabled façades attract millions of visitors annually. The [[Stock exchange|Amsterdam Stock Exchange]], founded in 1602, is considered the oldest 'modern' securities market. Many large Dutch institutions and multinational companies have headquarters in the city, and it is the cultural capital of the Netherlands. The government and foreign embassies are in [[The Hague]], not Amsterdam. The city is known for openness, liberalism and tolerance, and for the art of [[Rembrandt]] and [[Vincent van Gogh]].

Main international airport of the [[Netherlands]], 9 km southwest of [[Amsterdam]]. It is the principal hub for [[KLM]] and its regional affiliate KLM Cityhopper. In 2025 it handled 68.8 million passengers, the fourth-busiest airport in Europe by passenger volume. Schiphol began as a military airfield on 19 September 1916. In 1949 it was decided that Schiphol would become the primary airport of the Netherlands. Passenger traffic fell sharply during the [[COVID-19 pandemic|COVID-19 pandemic]] and had not returned to its 2019 record by 2025.

National passenger railroad company of the United States, doing business as Amtrak. Founded in 1971 as a quasi-public corporation, it receives federal and state subsidies but is managed as a for-profit organization. It operates intercity rail service in every contiguous U.S. state except [[Wyoming]] and [[South Dakota]], as well as in three Canadian provinces. Its headquarters is in [[Washington, D.C.]] In fiscal year 2025 it served 34.5 million passengers, with more than 22,100 employees. The name is a portmanteau of 'America' and 'track'.

Major river of [[Central Asia]], historically known as the Oxus. It rises in the Pamir Mountains, north of the [[Hindu Kush]], and is formed by the confluence of the Vakhsh and Panj rivers. It flows through [[Afghanistan]], [[Tajikistan]], [[Turkmenistan]] and [[Uzbekistan]], and has a total length of 2,400 kilometers (1,500 mi). Historically it flowed north-west into the [[Aral Sea]], but today it does not reach the sea, and its mouth lies in a dried-up area of what was the Aral Sea. Large-scale [[Irrigation|irrigation]] has greatly reduced its flow. The river is navigable for over 1,450 kilometers (900 mi). In ancient history it was regarded as the boundary of Greater Iran with Turan.

Major ancient Egyptian deity and member of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad. His oracle at Siwa Oasis, in western Egypt, remained the only oracle of Amun throughout. From the 11th Dynasty (c. 21st century BC) he was patron deity of Thebes, replacing Montu. After the rebellion of Thebes against the Hyksos, under [[Ahmose I|Ahmose I]] (16th century BC), he was fused with the sun god [[Ra]] as Amun-Ra and gained national importance. As chief deity of the New Kingdom (16th–11th centuries BC), Amun-Ra was the champion of the poor or troubled and central to personal piety, except during the Atenist heresy of [[Akhenaten]]. He was identified with [[Zeus]] in Greece and [[Jupiter (god)|Jupiter]] in Rome, and was worshiped in [[Nubia]].
